summary: Give your composer a concrete existing song as a starting point, but don't let you or them get fixated on it, because a new piece has to do more than imitate the reference.
takeaways: Concrete reference tracks give composers a clear starting point
Say which qualities of the reference to keep and drop
Fixating on one reference produces cheap imitations
License an existing song if it fits perfectly
games: Ore no Shikabane wo Koete Yuke

principles.principle: Give composers a reference track and name what to keep from it
principles.why: A concrete example helps a composer know where to start, but composers often can't tell which parts of a reference to keep or change, which is a common way to lose sight of the goal.
principles.how: Name the quality you want (e.g., the surfer feel of The Ventures) and the signature parts not to copy (e.g., the famous guitar riff).
principles.anti_pattern: Handing over a song with only "make it like this".
principles.example: God Hand's "Gene's Rock-a-Bye" was asked for in the style of The Ventures; the iconic riff was left out but the surfer sound stayed.

principles.principle: Don't let one reference track close off other musical possibilities
principles.why: A director fixated on a single piece closes their mind to alternatives, and everything ends up sounding like a cheap imitation.
principles.how: Treat the reference as a starting point and judge drafts by how well they serve the game, staying flexible about the result.
principles.anti_pattern: Rejecting every draft that doesn't sound like the reference.
principles.quote: Everything will sound like a cheap imitation— and you can't lock yourself down like that.

principles.principle: License an existing song when it matches the game's theme exactly
principles.why: Sometimes an existing piece fits a game's theme so well that using it as-is beats any soundalike.
principles.how: Negotiate with the rightsholders to use the original song.
principles.example: Ore no Shikabane wo Koete Yuke uses "Hana", a song about flowers blooming and wilting, for a family cursed with a two-year lifespan; designer Mr. Masuda negotiated the rights.

summary: Use brief full-screen flashes for impact and character flashes to show status changes, and build dark elements into character flashes so they keep their contrast instead of fading into the background.
takeaways: Full-screen flashes add impact like screen shake
Character flashes emphasize status changes
Plain white flashes lose contrast on light backgrounds
Add shadows to flashes for internal contrast
Scale flash strength with camera distance

principles.principle: Give character hit flashes internal contrast, not just added white
principles.why: Adding one color evenly raises dark and light areas equally so contrast averages out, and white flashes make characters vanish on light backgrounds.
principles.how: Mix dark or shadow elements into the flash, as Smash Ultimate does, so the character stays readable on any background.
principles.anti_pattern: Simply brightening the character when they get hit.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate added shadows to its hit flash, based on a mockup Sakurai drew for the team.
principles.quote: If you simply brighten a character when they get hit, they'll vanish into the background like this.

principles.principle: Use distinct flash colors to signal each character status
principles.why: Making a character flash emphasizes a change in that character's status.
principles.how: Assign one treatment per status and keep it consistent: e.g., white for invulnerability, yellow for can't-be-grabbed-again after a throw, rim lighting for damage types.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: white flash when invulnerable while getting up, yellow flash after being thrown, rim lighting for invulnerability.

principles.principle: Use brief full-screen flashes for impact, scaled by camera distance
principles.why: Like screen shake, a flash covering the whole screen adds impact through its large area, but a strong flash when zoomed in makes too much of the screen flash.
principles.how: Keep flashes to a single brief moment, lower their strength when the camera is close, and check them on LCD screens, whose response times change how they look.
principles.anti_pattern: Full-strength or long flashes with the camera zoomed in.
principles.quote: considering the impact they add, they're worth taking the time to perfect.

summary: When supervising art, give precise, drawn feedback until an asset clearly reads as what it should be, and when repeated rounds still fall short, accept it and move on.
takeaways: Give art feedback with retouched reference images
Even spacing and copy-paste make breaks look fake
Judge assets by their core goal, not your mental image
Ship it as-is when repeated feedback stops converging

principles.principle: Give art feedback as paint-overs with specific, concrete fixes
principles.why: Retouched images made it much clearer what Sakurai wanted than words alone, and specific notes let the team act on each problem.
principles.how: Draw over deliveries and name exact changes: avoid perpendicular cuts, keep the X-axis flat, make spacing erratic, vary copy-pasted patterns.
principles.anti_pattern: Vague notes like "make it look better".
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Mishima Dojo destructible wall went through several rounds of retouched feedback images.

principles.principle: Judge assets by their core purpose, not by your mental image
principles.why: The wall only had to look like wooden boards had actually been broken; work that differs from the director's picture is fine if the quality is there.
principles.how: State each asset's goal in one sentence and approve anything that meets it.
principles.anti_pattern: Forcing every asset to conform to the director's personal ideal.
principles.quote: My goal isn't to make everything in the game conform to my ideals, so I make these decisions surprisingly often.

principles.principle: Accept and ship an asset when repeated feedback stops converging
principles.why: Supervision often yields a half-step when you hoped for a whole step, and big swings each round feel like changing direction; the director and artist share responsibility.
principles.how: After several rounds without reaching the bar, put the asset in the game as-is and move on.
principles.anti_pattern: Changing direction with every round of feedback.
principles.quote: Whenever such cases arise... it's best to accept it and move on.

principles.principle: Make broken objects irregular and check them from gameplay distance
principles.why: Even spacing, square outlines and copy-pasted shapes made the wall look manufactured, and some of these only showed from far away; low splinters also intruded into the fighters' path.
principles.how: Vary spacing and shapes, review at the gameplay camera distance, and keep debris out of the space characters move through.
principles.anti_pattern: Evenly spaced, perpendicular or repeated breaks.
principles.example: Mishima Dojo wall: evenly spaced beams and a square-looking hole from afar; splinters raised out of the fighters' path.

summary: Animators must always know when and where an attack's collision is active, so the animation lines up with the hitbox and the strongest pose lands on the hit frame.
takeaways: Fast games need hitboxes wider than the weapon
Attacks must cross the line where opponents stand
Start collision when the pose looks strongest
Animators share responsibility for game feel

principles.principle: Make attack collision wider than the visible weapon in fast games
principles.why: With fast, coordinate-based movement, hitboxes mapped tightly to a sword or fist make attacks miss and players get more and more stressed.
principles.how: Extend hitboxes beyond the weapon and make sure every attack's range crosses the median line where opponents stand.
principles.anti_pattern: Hitboxes that exactly match the blade or fist.
principles.example: Smash Bros. attack collision covers a wider range than the fighter's sword or fist.

principles.principle: Line up the strongest attack pose with the first active collision frame
principles.why: The clean-hit frame is where hitstop happens and players get a clear view, and on finishing blows the screen stops completely, so a weak pose there looks bad.
principles.how: Start collision partway through a swing, once the pose is strong, rather than at the first frame of motion.
principles.anti_pattern: Collision that starts during a weak wind-up pose.
principles.example: Smash Bros. sword swings: collision doesn't start until the sword is partway through the swing.
principles.quote: Weak attack poses are no good in these situations.

principles.principle: Keep attack animations positioned where the collision actually is
principles.why: A designer can make any animation connect, but a large gap between visuals and collision feels broken; some mismatch is fine if it makes the game more fun.
principles.how: Have animators work with hitbox timing and placement visible, and review attacks with collision displayed.
principles.anti_pattern: Fixing a misplaced animation by stretching the hitbox to meet it.
principles.quote: When crafting attack animations, it's important that the animators are always aware of when and where collision occurs.

summary: Don't let targeting and market research generate your new game ideas: they only describe paths others have already taken, and following them leads to average games in crowded markets.
takeaways: Market data describes the past, not what comes next
Audience boundaries by age and gender are blurry
Target "beginners", not a specific age range
Following the main road yields mediocre, lower-selling games

principles.principle: Don't let market research generate your new game ideas
principles.why: Research is built on finished products and only shows the safe main road; following it makes work more average and mediocre, and it sells less.
principles.how: Form the concept first and use data only to check risks; ask what a booming genre will look like when you release.
principles.anti_pattern: Chasing whatever genre the data says is selling now.
principles.example: Around the NES-to-SNES transition, many Japanese companies made Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy-like RPGs and dove into an overcrowded market.
principles.quote: Targeting and market research data is built on everything that's come before. They don't show the path to what comes next.

principles.principle: Target players by experience level, not by age or gender
principles.why: Audience lines are blurry: some older people like cute things and some kids prefer intense content, and "beginners" spans all ages and genders.
principles.how: Define the audience by need (e.g., beginners) and still give the controls enough depth that advanced players enjoy them.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating demographic slices as hard boundaries.
principles.example: The original Kirby was designed for beginners, never "for children", yet advanced players enjoy how it controls.
principles.quote: So if I had to name a target audience, it would be "beginners." Not any specific age range.

summary: Live, one-time stakes, such as a real chance of failing in front of an audience, are what make a gameplay performance thrilling and memorable.
takeaways: Sakurai played Uprising live with an orchestra at PRESS START 2012
Max difficulty and no restarts made failure a real risk
The orchestra followed his mid-boss timing
One-time live performances are special because they're unrepeatable

principles.principle: Keep real failure stakes when showing gameplay to a live audience
principles.why: The chance that a Game Over would end the performance with no restart made it a one-of-a-kind thrill, and audience feedback said exactly that.
principles.how: Play at high difficulty with no restarts so the audience senses genuine risk, as Sakurai did at Intensity 9.0 with zero defense.
principles.example: PRESS START 2012: Kid Icarus: Uprising Chapter 12 Air Battle played live with the orchestra.
principles.quote: The heart and soul of PRESS START is that everything was done live. It was meant to be enjoyed there alone.

principles.principle: Plan music cues around gameplay segments of variable length
principles.why: The Chapter 12 clear time depended on how fast the mid-boss died, so the orchestra had to align its performance with when Sakurai beat it.
principles.how: Identify segments whose length varies and give the music cue points that wait for or follow the player's actual progress.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Air Battles last five minutes, but the mid-boss made the exact timing vary.

summary: Notice when you're only hearing agreement about your ideas, designs or reviews, and stay objective, while still keeping the conviction to push your game in its own deliberately "unbalanced" direction.
takeaways: Agreement online reinforces views while dissenters stay unseen
Echo chambers affect design ideas and reviews daily
Without objectivity, a game ends up unbalanced
A deliberate unique direction still beats being swayed

principles.principle: Seek out opinions from outside the circle that agrees with you
principles.why: A flood of agreement makes you feel right even though many people disagree, and an insular world makes you lose sight of problems that need solving.
principles.how: When judging design ideas or reviews, check whether you're only seeing approval, and deliberately ask people outside that community.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting in only the opinions that validate you.
principles.quote: You might play things safer, or you may push it further— and in either case, if you can't stay objective, your game will surely end up unbalanced.

principles.principle: Keep your deliberate unique direction while adapting to team concerns
principles.why: Going in your own "unbalanced" direction can feel best and beats being swayed by others, since a unique vision gives a game distinctive strength, but balance still matters.
principles.how: Listen to and adapt to your team's concerns, but don't sand off the distinctive choices just to please outside voices.
principles.anti_pattern: Being swayed by others until the game loses its identity.
principles.quote: when making games, sometimes taking things in your own "unbalanced" direction is what feels best!

summary: Add help text to menu items, write it in different words than the item's name, and trim it until its meaning is clear at a glance.
takeaways: Add help text to every menu item
Never explain an option using its own name
Cut excess words; translate meaning, not words
Avoid jargon like "config" or "key repeat"

principles.principle: Never explain a menu item using the item's own name
principles.why: Help text exists for players who don't know what the term means, so repeating the name misses the point, and Sakurai says it happens quite often.
principles.how: Rewrite with different words: "Options" becomes "Adjust a variety of game settings."
principles.anti_pattern: Help text like "Go to the Options."
principles.quote: This is important, so I'll say it again: don't explain using the same words!

principles.principle: Polish help text and mode names down to their plain meaning
principles.why: Being immediately clear in a few words is hard, so you must drill down to the most important part, and not everyone knows technical terms.
principles.how: Cut excess words, translate meaning rather than words, prefer "Play Solo" over "1P Mode", and replace terms like "config" or "key repeat".
principles.anti_pattern: Technical terminology in menus.

principles.principle: Add help text to menus proactively
principles.why: Menu items are usually one or two words that often don't say what they do; Sakurai considers help text relatively vital and has used it in almost all his games.
principles.how: Show a one-line description of the highlighted item, for example at the bottom of the screen.

summary: In strategy games, start from symmetric fairness, then build push and pull through counters, costs, abilities and range, so the fun comes from out-configuring an evenly matched opponent.
takeaways: Identical armies should draw, or it isn't fair
Winning through better configuration is the core essence
Counter cycles need clear weaknesses and fitting costs
Range and position create push and pull too
Random evasion is optional and can feel unfair

principles.principle: Make mirror matches draw, then reward smarter army configuration
principles.why: Identical armies must draw for the game to be fair, and the fun of strategy is changing your setup to beat an even opponent decisively.
principles.how: Test mirror matchups for balance, then make sure composition choices clearly tip the outcome.
principles.anti_pattern: A built-in advantage for one side.
principles.example: Rock, Paper, Scissors: identical teams draw.
principles.quote: Changing your configuration to achieve a crushing victory is the fundamental game essence found in strategy games.

principles.principle: Build counter cycles with clear weaknesses and fitting resource costs
principles.why: Clear strengths, weaknesses and appropriate costs enrich the game, and differences in power or abilities add depth.
principles.how: Create cycles like infantry, tanks, helicopters, anti-air, and vary units by cost, attack power and abilities such as leaping over others.
principles.anti_pattern: Adding complexity without allocating strengths and weaknesses wisely.
principles.example: Infantry lose to tanks, tanks to helicopters, helicopters to anti-air cannons, anti-air to infantry.

principles.principle: Use attack range and position as a source of push and pull
principles.why: In shogi and chess the push and pull comes from attack range, not strength, and long-range or map-based weapons make holding good positions the core.
principles.how: Give units distinct ranges and make positioning matter as much as raw power.
principles.example: Shogi and chess: tension comes from attack range and position.

principles.principle: Question whether random evasion is needed in strategy combat
principles.why: A game will likely work without random dodge chances; they keep players on their toes but can feel unfair.
principles.how: Prototype without randomness first, and add it only if the uncertainty is worth the unfairness it brings.
principles.anti_pattern: Random rolls that swing the same battle unpredictably.

summary: Treat post-launch patches as a bonus, not a plan: modern games will ship with bugs that only the market finds, but no patch helps once players have given up, so ship in the best shape you can.
takeaways: Modern games are vastly more complex and unstable
Developers barely get to play the finished game
The market finds rare bugs testing can't
Balance and quality-of-life patches are a bonus
Patches can't win back players who already quit

principles.principle: Ship in the best possible shape; patches can't recover lost players
principles.why: No matter how much a game improves through patches, it means nothing if players have already given up on it.
principles.how: Set your release quality bar as if no update will come.
principles.anti_pattern: Shipping rough and planning to fix it later.
principles.quote: no matter how much you improve your game through patches, it won't mean anything if your players have already given up on the game.

principles.principle: Fix crash bugs first; treat balance and QoL patches as optional
principles.why: Fatal bugs must be fixed, but balance tweaks and quality-of-life features are a free bonus that ties up the director and key staff who could start the next game.
principles.how: Triage post-launch work by severity and weigh optional updates against freeing the core team.

principles.principle: Plan for the market to find bugs your testers can't
principles.why: A one-in-a-thousand bug is unlikely to show up in testing, every fix restarts checking from scratch, and after launch players put the game through far more.
principles.how: Lock content early to get time with near-final builds, and watch player videos and reports after launch as a major test pass.
principles.example: A bug only one in a thousand players hits can be uploaded as a video once the game is out.

summary: Borrow manga and anime's non-realistic conventions, like putting the mouth on the side of the face in profile, whenever they express a character better than realism would.
takeaways: Manga conventions can express characters better than realism
Side-placed mouths read well and allow cel swaps
Some cartoon effects are hard in CG
Question your givens to find more expressive visuals

principles.principle: Use non-realistic manga conventions when they express characters better
principles.why: Lacking realism is no reason to avoid these techniques; a mouth moved to the side of a face is unnatural but a great way to express a character.
principles.how: In profile shots, try placing the mouth on the side of the face and judge by expressiveness rather than anatomy.
principles.anti_pattern: Rejecting a technique only because it isn't realistic.
principles.example: Mega Man Legends cutscenes and Sonic put the mouth on the side of the face in profile.

principles.principle: Swap mouth cels for profile lip movement instead of animating jaws
principles.why: Moving the mouth by swapping cels is easier to produce and may make mouth movement easier to read.
principles.how: Use texture or cel swaps for the mouth in profile shots rather than rigging jaw motion.
principles.example: Mega Man Legends shows mouth movement in profile by swapping cels without animating the jaw.

principles.principle: Question inherited modeling conventions; you can't fix what you don't notice
principles.why: Kirby's and Jigglypuff's mouths were first modeled in an older style; Sakurai's requested design is less anatomically true but more expressive.
principles.how: Review models at the angles players see and challenge any default that reads less expressively.
principles.anti_pattern: Taking default designs for granted.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: Kirby and Jigglypuff mouths remodeled to Sakurai's request.
principles.quote: don't take your givens as givens, and instead look for a suitable—or even exaggerated—way of expressing your visuals.

summary: Use cutscenes where they add emotion, clarity or a breather, but respect the player's time: keep them tight, always let players skip them (credits included), ideally add fast-forward, and use quick-time events with great caution.
takeaways: Long, irrelevant cutscenes make players impatient
Cutscenes can carry emotion gameplay can't
Always allow skipping, including the credits
Offer fast-forward like sped-up video viewing
Use quick-time events with extreme caution

principles.principle: Always let players skip cutscenes, credits included
principles.why: Even on a first playthrough it may not be the player's first time seeing the scene, and unskippable cutscenes feel off-putting.
principles.how: Put a skip option on every cutscene and the credits from the first playthrough.
principles.anti_pattern: Locking cutscenes until the second playthrough.
principles.quote: On a related note, players should always be able to skip cutscenes. That includes the credits.

principles.principle: Add fast-forward to cutscenes, not just a skip button
principles.why: Dialogue scenes can be skipped line by line, and people now watch videos sped up on DVRs and YouTube, so cutscenes should adapt to today's needs.
principles.how: Let players skip ahead or fast-forward within a cutscene.

principles.principle: Keep cutscenes short unless they carry emotion or clarity
principles.why: Long irrelevant cutscenes make players impatient, but cutscenes can tell a story more clearly, build emotional investment and give a breather; as rewards they lose value because they end up online.
principles.how: Trim irrelevant scenes, reserve long ones for moments gameplay can't convey, and don't rely on cutscenes as the reward for good play.
principles.anti_pattern: Long stretches of relatively irrelevant cutscenes.

principles.principle: Use quick-time events in cutscenes with extreme caution
principles.why: Quick-time events seem to be quite unpopular, even if the aim is to keep players on edge.
principles.how: Test any QTE with players before committing, and cut it if it frustrates them.
principles.anti_pattern: QTEs added just to keep people on the edge of their seats.

summary: Give a project one director who owns the content and concept, and a producer who owns money, staffing and marketing, and make sure both are working toward the same quality goal.
takeaways: Directors have the final call on content
Usually one director, to avoid split opinions
Producers handle budget, staffing and marketing
Both roles share the goal of a quality product

principles.principle: Keep one director with clear final say over content
principles.why: The director sets the game's direction, and multiple directors cause split opinions and unclear goals.
principles.how: Name one director; if you divide the role, state explicitly who has the final say on what.
principles.anti_pattern: Shared directing with no clear decision-maker.
principles.quote: Usually, a team has one director. That's because the role entails charting a game's path, and you don't want split opinions or unclear goals.

principles.principle: Let the director come up with the game's concept
principles.why: Designing a concept is difficult without a grasp of the game's core appeal, which the director needs to hold.
principles.how: Have the director originate the concept, even if a game designer later fleshes out the design.
principles.anti_pattern: Separating the concept from the person who charts the game's path.

principles.principle: Give producers budget, staffing and publicity so directors can focus
principles.why: Producers weigh dev costs against projected sales and handle marketing, because a good game doesn't matter if nobody knows about it, while directors are very busy.
principles.how: Assign a producer to financing, staffing and interviews, and build mutual trust so the director-producer split doesn't become a standoff.
principles.example: Sakurai often takes on a producer's role himself, since Smash fighter reveal movies are marketing.

summary: Open your game with a climactic scene the player controls and save the backstory for later, because players want to take control and discover the game right away.
takeaways: The intro is extremely important
Lead with a climactic event; explain how later
Let players take control first thing
Show early that the enemy means business
If no climax fits, keep the opening short

principles.principle: Open with a climactic, playable scene instead of backstory
principles.why: Players want to take control and find out about the game, and many games start slowly with backstory, customs and relationships.
principles.how: Put the player in control of a dramatic scene in the first minutes, and explain how things got there later.
principles.anti_pattern: Spending a long time on backstory before letting players play.
principles.example: Final Fantasy VII opens like the run-up to a final dungeon instead of explaining why Cloud joined Avalanche.
principles.quote: With games in particular, players really want to take control and find out about your game— so it's no time for ambling along. Let them play, first thing!

principles.principle: Show early that the enemy means business
principles.why: A speedy start that introduces the threat immediately hooks players, while lore can be skimmed and filled in later.
principles.how: Introduce the main antagonist within about the first minute and defer secondary details.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising Chapter 1 throws you into an Air Battle and introduces Medusa in under a minute.

principles.principle: If you can't open on a peak, keep the opening short
principles.why: Letting events unfold through daily life is fine, but players should get control as soon as possible.
principles.how: Shorten any everyday-life opening and hand control to the player early.
principles.anti_pattern: A long, slow opening before the first input.
principles.example: Phoenix Wright puts you into a trial at the very start.

summary: Don't let convenient tools like realistic skeleton rigs decide what your animation can do; great animation goes beyond real-world limits.
takeaways: FK and IK are long-standing rigging fundamentals
Joints stop at 180 degrees; Sakurai wants more
Extra joints cost processing and cartoon-minded animators
Convenient systems create false mental limits

principles.principle: Push key poses beyond realistic joint limits for extra oomph
principles.why: Pushing beyond common sense is what gives animation its greatness, and bending past a straight arm adds oomph.
principles.how: Try extending limbs past straight in strong attack poses and check whether your rig allows it.
principles.anti_pattern: Stopping at realistic joint limits by default.
principles.quote: In any case, I'd say that pushing beyond common sense is what gives animation its greatness.

principles.principle: Plan rigs for cartoon exaggeration at the start of development
principles.why: Joints that bend backward are harder to use (IK may flip), and fixes like extra joints add processing load and need cartoon-minded animators.
principles.how: Decide early if the style needs exaggeration, then budget for extra joints and brief or hire animators with cartoon sensibilities.
principles.example: Sakurai suggested exaggerated rigs at the start of Smash Bros. development, but processing load and staffing left it unsolved.

principles.principle: Don't let convenient tools set the limits of your ideas
principles.why: If you're too tied to convenient systems, you struggle to step away from them and form mental boundaries about what's possible.
principles.how: Regularly ask which "impossible" ideas are only limits of a tool, and push past them.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating a standard tool's defaults as the boundary of what's possible.
principles.quote: If you're too tied down to convenient systems, you'll end up struggling to step away from their convenience.

summary: When you're stuck for an idea, define the theme of the problem first, then generate as many candidate solutions as you can, following each thread before you prune.
takeaways: Keep thinking instead of waiting for inspiration
Define the problem's theme first
Generate many solutions; quantity over quality
Follow weak ideas to workable variants

principles.principle: Define the problem's theme before you start generating ideas
principles.why: Thinking of something from nothing leaves no clear starting point, so ideas naturally won't come.
principles.how: Write the problem as a simple one-line theme, e.g., "how to put out a fire in some ruins."
principles.anti_pattern: Brainstorming with no defined problem.
principles.quote: If you try to think of something from nothing, you won't have a clear starting point. And then it'll only be natural if the ideas won't come.

principles.principle: Generate many solutions first and prune them later
principles.why: Even unrealistic ideas are better than none; quantity gets you past the feeling of having nothing and opens the path to improvements.
principles.how: List broad solution types, including silly ones, and note why each fails in context before cutting any.
principles.anti_pattern: Discarding minor or silly ideas too early.
principles.quote: Quantity over quality— save the pruning for later.

principles.principle: Mine rejected ideas for variants that fix their flaws
principles.why: Following each thread instead of passing over minor ideas can lead to an answer.
principles.how: For each failed idea, ask what tweak would make it work (no sand, try dirt; bucket too small, try a bigger one).
principles.example: Fire in ruins: sand is hard to find but dirt might work; a bigger bucket might work.

summary: Set difficulty, rewards and penalties by asking how good or bad the player's action really was, so consequences feel earned, while leaving room for deliberate surprises.
takeaways: Scale consequences to how good the action was
Risky, slow attacks deserve bigger payoffs
Decide whether bad irreversible choices can be redeemed
Too strict a mapping makes games predictable
Rare lucrative, hard-to-beat enemies make special goals

principles.principle: Scale rewards and penalties to how good the action really was
principles.why: Players are happiest when their behavior is compensated correctly, and success and failure should each have a fitting consequence.
principles.how: For each reward, penalty and damage value, ask how good or bad the triggering action was; give more points for stronger, harder enemies.
principles.anti_pattern: Pushing the mapping so far that the game becomes predictable.
principles.example: Score games award more points by enemy strength and difficulty, and can add location-based damage or breakable parts.

principles.principle: Give slower, riskier attacks proportionally bigger payoffs
principles.why: A move that takes time and leaves you open is harder to land, so landing it is more commendable and should pay off more.
principles.how: Give high-startup, high-commitment moves more damage and knockback than quick, safe ones.
principles.example: Smash Bros.: quick neutral attacks versus slow, vulnerable smash attacks with more damage and knockback.
principles.quote: Landing a hit with the latter is a more commendable feat, so we've given it the damage and knockback such a feat deserves.

principles.principle: Decide how players can recover from bad irreversible choices
principles.why: A big penalty for a really bad action can be fun, but you must ask whether the player can ever redeem themselves and how much effort it takes.
principles.how: Review irreversible choices by how bad the action was, not just scenario logic, and set an explicit path and cost to recover.
principles.anti_pattern: Permanent penalties decided only by scenario logic.

principles.principle: Break the reward rules deliberately with rare, hard-to-beat targets
principles.why: Polishing every consequence can make a game predictable; an unusually lucrative enemy that is hard to beat becomes a special objective.
principles.how: Add an occasional high-value enemy with high HP or a tendency to flee.

summary: A Grab Bag-style history of the Famicom's five sound channels and the expansion hardware that changed its music across regions, showing how hard limits shaped game audio.
takeaways: Famicom: two pulse, triangle, noise and DPCM channels
Music and sound effects shared the same channels
DPCM sampling grew with larger cartridge ROMs
Missing expansion audio changed music overseas

principles.principle: Decide which music voice yields when sound effects need a channel
principles.why: On the Famicom, music and sound effects shared the same five channels, so part of the music often cut out when an effect played.
principles.how: When voices are limited, set a priority so the least important music part drops out for an effect.
principles.example: Famicom games cut part of the music to play sound effects.

principles.principle: Match each sound role to the timbre that suits it
principles.why: Crisp pulse waves carried most Famicom music, the mellow triangle wave suited bass lines, and noise suited hits, explosions, cheers and waves.
principles.how: Assign tones by role: crisp tones for main parts, mellow tones for bass, noise for impacts and ambient effects.

principles.principle: Check that audio features exist on every hardware version you ship
principles.why: The NES lacked the cartridge pins for expansion audio and the Disk System stayed in Japan, so several games' music felt different overseas.
principles.how: List the audio features each target platform or region supports and provide fallbacks; larger ROMs later let DPCM close the gap.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on audio hardware only some versions have.
principles.example: Several Famicom games sounded different from their NES versions without expansion chips.

summary: Make your game playable without reading a word: put pictures on menu icons, and make repeated presses of the confirm button lead straight into the main game.
takeaways: Aim for games playable without reading any words
Put pictures or characters on menu icons
Repeated confirm presses should reach the main game
Set this up deliberately, not by accident

principles.principle: Make menus usable without reading any text
principles.why: Pictures on icons are more fun to look at and help players work out what each one does, even in a language they can't read.
principles.how: Add a picture or character to each major menu icon, then test the menus in a language you can't read.
principles.anti_pattern: Text-only menus that become unusable without the language.
principles.example: With the menus switched to Korean, the pictures on each icon still help comprehension somewhat.
principles.quote: Ideally, games should be playable even if you can't read a single word.

principles.principle: Let repeated confirm presses lead straight into the main game
principles.why: A player who can't read anything can still start playing, and Sakurai sets this up on purpose rather than leaving it to chance.
principles.how: Set default cursor positions from the title screen onward so mashing confirm reaches the main mode, tutorial included.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate reaches Smash mode's fighter select, Kirby Air Ride the first Air Ride stage, and Kirby Super Star the first scenario with tutorial.

summary: You can turn any single-player game into a head-to-head contest: two players start the same game at the same moment and race to a shared goal or to see who fails first.
takeaways: Start the same game simultaneously on two screens
First to fail loses, or the higher score wins
Set short goals for slow games
Visible opponent progress makes it heated
Move straight to the next game after each result

principles.principle: Create competition by racing players through identical content simultaneously
principles.why: Starting the same game at the same time turns even non-competitive games into contests, especially arcade games where one mistake ends your run.
principles.how: Start both players together and decide the winner by first failure, higher score, progress or a set goal.
principles.example: Sakurai and Arino Kacho started each game together in the Retro Game Master crossover.

principles.principle: Show each player the opponent's progress to raise tension
principles.why: A simple race gets heated when you can see how far your opponent has gotten.
principles.how: Keep both screens or a progress indicator visible to both players in race or versus modes.
principles.quote: It might seem simple, but things get pretty heated when you can see how far your opponent has gotten.

principles.principle: Give long games short, concrete win goals for competitive play
principles.why: Even a slow game like Dragon Quest becomes competitive with a short goal, and moving straight to the next game keeps sessions varied.
principles.how: Define quick objectives like "first to beat three slimes" and switch games as soon as someone wins or fails.
principles.example: Dragon Quest: "the first to beat three slimes is the winner!"

summary: Lower the barrier to entry for new players from the first moment until they're hooked, without over-explaining, because a beginner who gets crushed or lectured will simply quit.
takeaways: Crushing a newcomer ruined their fun, and Sakurai regretted it
Going easy is fine unless they want full effort
Lower the barrier until players are drawn in
Too much hand-holding feels like being dragged along

principles.principle: Lower the barrier to entry until new players are fully drawn in
principles.why: There's no point in playing if you're not having fun, and it's hard enough to get people to play at all, so beginners who get crushed may abandon the game.
principles.how: Audit the path from first boot until a player is hooked, in single-player and competitive modes, and remove barriers along it.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting newcomers be flattened before they understand the game.
principles.example: The King of Fighters '95: Sakurai crushed a couple who had just come to try the game, and has mostly avoided playing strangers since.
principles.quote: Ultimately, there's no point in playing games if you're not having fun. As such, it's important to be kind when introducing new players to a title.

principles.principle: Avoid hand-holding that makes new players feel pulled along
principles.why: If everyone keeps telling players how to play, they feel dragged along and won't enjoy themselves.
principles.how: Limit tutorials and prompts, and leave enough freedom for players to get into the game on their own.
principles.anti_pattern: Constant instructions that take away the player's own discovery.
principles.quote: You want to give them enough freedom to get into the game themselves.

summary: Establish a character with an exaggerated, readable silhouette and strong poses, and make sure everyone working on them understands the character's core essence and pushes it further.
takeaways: Matching a reference isn't enough; capture the character
Exaggerate the silhouette, even in solid black
Poses change how the same character feels
Everyone on a character must understand its essence

principles.principle: Exaggerate silhouettes so characters read even in solid black
principles.why: The silhouette is the part Sakurai would stress most; an ambiguous, unreadable or indistinct one isn't good enough.
principles.how: Fill each character in black, check it's exaggerated and distinct from the cast, and emphasize signature features like hair, ribbons or head size.
principles.anti_pattern: Silhouettes that blend in with other characters.
principles.example: Nakoruru's emphasized hair, ribbon, gloves and legs, and Sonic's large head and exaggerated skinny limbs.
principles.quote: Their form should be exaggerated, even when they're just solid black. If the silhouette is ambiguous and unreadable, or impossible to distinguish from other characters, it's not good enough.

principles.principle: Pose characters to express who they are
principles.why: Depending on how well they're posed, the same character can look and feel completely different.
principles.how: Review each character's key poses and rework any that don't convey their personality.

principles.principle: Make sure everyone on a character understands its core essence
principles.why: Matching a source design isn't enough; the people assigned need to understand the essence and draw it out further, which takes the whole team.
principles.how: Write a short statement of each character's essence, share it with the team, and blend classic and newer design details when adapting.
principles.anti_pattern: Copying a reference design literally but missing what makes the character feel like themselves.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Mii Fighter Nakoruru costume matched KOF XIV but felt off until it was revised.

summary: Particles always cost processing, so get the most out of each one: keep them short and fast, pack several into one billboard, stagger their timing and positions, and draw them large.
takeaways: Particles always have a processing cost
Keep them short-lived and make up with speed
Pack multiple particles into one billboard
Stagger timing and position; draw them large
Hand-animated effects save processing on weak hardware

principles.principle: Keep particles short-lived and compensate with higher speed
principles.why: New particles need to appear quickly, so lingering after-effects aren't affordable.
principles.how: Shorten particle lifetimes and increase their velocity so bursts still read.
principles.anti_pattern: Long-lived particles crowding the screen.

principles.principle: Pack several particles into one large billboard
principles.why: Many tiny particles cost too much, so each billboard must be used as effectively as possible.
principles.how: Draw clusters (e.g., several bubbles) onto one panel and make each billboard somewhat large.
principles.anti_pattern: Spawning many tiny individual particles.
principles.example: Steel Diver's projectile bubbles are a few panels, each containing several bubbles.

principles.principle: Stagger particle spawn timing and positions to avoid waste
principles.why: Staggering timing reduces how many particles are on screen at once, and overlapping particles are wasted.
principles.how: Offset spawn times across emitters that fire together and spread out spawn positions.
principles.anti_pattern: Particles stacked on top of each other.

principles.principle: Use pre-authored or pattern-based effects when processing is scarce
principles.why: Hand-placed frame animations cost ROM but very little processing, and work within the hardware's limits.
principles.how: Bake effects as frame animations or pick randomly from preset motion patterns, mixing light and dark pixels for visibility on any background.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land: enemy-defeat stars and explosions hand-placed per frame; the inhale effect plays from set patterns.
principles.quote: All you can do is work within your game's limits and try to aim for the best effect possible.

summary: If people don't "get" your game, explain its essence to players directly and regularly, ideally in the words of the person who knows it best, because an unknown game might as well not exist.
takeaways: Explain a misunderstood game directly to players
Daily updates turn checking in into a habit
The person who knows the game best should shape messaging
Development and marketing are two wheels on one axle

principles.principle: Explain a misunderstood game's essence directly to players
principles.why: The original Smash's rules, controls and feel were unlike earlier fighting games, so people dismissed it before release, and a document sent to magazines had little impact.
principles.how: Write a plain guide to the game's essence and unique features and publish it directly to players.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying only on press coverage to explain an unusual game.
principles.example: Sakurai turned "The Secrets of Smash Bros." into the Smash Bros. DOJO!! site, built himself in an HTML editor.

principles.principle: Post updates on a fixed, frequent schedule fans can rely on
principles.why: People came to the site excited to see something new, which works well once it becomes a daily routine.
principles.how: Release one new detail on a set schedule (e.g., every weekday) and plan localization early for a global audience.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Brawl's Dojo posted five times a week in six languages.

principles.principle: Have the person who knows the game best shape its messaging
principles.why: The director knows the content and its fun best; delegating still means briefing on every post and reviewing it.
principles.how: Delegate production tasks like screenshots, but have the director write or review public explanations.
principles.example: During Melee's brutal development, Sakurai updated the Dojo himself and replied to comments.

principles.principle: Treat development and marketing as equally necessary parts of shipping
principles.why: No matter how good a game is, nobody plays it if nobody knows about it, and today information has to reach people scrolling social media.
principles.how: Plan how each piece of news will reach players' feeds alongside development milestones.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating marketing as separate from development.
principles.example: Mr. Sakurai Presents videos are another way he delivers information.
principles.quote: I see development and marketing as two wheels on one axle. No matter how good something is, an unknown game might as well not exist.
